questions.stem: Place the hyperkalemia treatments in order of how quickly they act on the heart and the serum potassium, from fastest to slowest.

items.text: Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate: binds potassium in the gut over hours
IV regular insulin with dextrose: shifts potassium into cells within 15 to 30 minutes
IV calcium gluconate: stabilizes the heart muscle within minutes
Nebulized albuterol: also shifts potassium into cells
Hemodialysis: removes potassium from the body

rationale.correct: Calcium protects the heart first, insulin and albuterol shift potassium, binders and dialysis remove it.

perOption.a: Protects the heart but does not lower potassium.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: The protocol orders regular insulin 0.1 units/kg (maximum 10 units) IV with 25 g of dextrose. The client weighs 84 kg. How many units of insulin should the nurse prepare? Round to the nearest whole unit.

rationale.correct: 0.1 x 84 = 8.4 units, rounded to 8 units per the protocol; below the 10-unit maximum. Many protocols now use 5 units in kidney failure to reduce hypoglycemia, and glucose is checked hourly for 4 to 6 hours.
references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

exhibits.title: Hyperkalemia protocol
exhibits.body: Calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL IV over 10 minutes. Regular insulin 0.1 units/kg IV (round to the nearest whole unit, maximum 10) with dextrose 50% 50 mL. Albuterol 10 mg nebulized. Emergency hemodialysis. Weight 84 kg.

questions.stem: Which actions should the nurse take while dialysis is arranged? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give calcium gluconate IV on a cardiac monitor
Check glucose every hour after the insulin
Raise the head of the bed and give oxygen
Avoid blood pressure checks and IV lines in the fistula arm
Give the client a banana for the hypoglycemia risk

rationale.correct: Stabilize the heart, watch glucose after insulin, treat the edema and protect the fistula.

perOption.b: Hypoglycemia is common, especially in kidney failure.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

exhibits.body: Vancomycin and ceftazidime intraperitoneally. Heparin 500 units/L in bags. Retrain technique.

questions.stem: The nurse retrains the client on a manual exchange. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Connect the new bag using aseptic technique without touching the connectors
Drain the used fluid, then fill with the new solution
Close windows, remove pets and clean the work surface
Put on a mask and perform hand hygiene
Inspect the drained fluid and record the volume
Check the bag: concentration, expiry, clarity and leaks

rationale.correct: Clean environment, mask and hands, check the bag, aseptic connection, drain then fill, inspect.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of acute kidney injury.

questions.stem: For each factor, indicate how it reduced kidney perfusion. Each row may have more than one answer.

rows.text: Hydrochlorothiazide
Diarrhea
Ibuprofen
Lisinopril

rationale.correct: Volume loss, NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors together (the triple whammy) collapse filtration pressure.

perOption.r4:c1: Blocks angiotensin II, which normally keeps filtration pressure up.

questions.educationalObjective: Take action for a nephrostomy problem.

questions.stem: The stone was calcium oxalate. Before discharge, for each statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or needs more teaching.

rows.text: "I'll drink enough to pass 2.5 liters of urine a day."
"I'll cut out all calcium foods."
"I'll eat less salt and fewer high-oxalate foods like spinach."
"I'll strain my urine and bring any stone in."
"I'll take vitamin C 2 grams daily for my immune system."

rationale.correct: Fluids, normal calcium, less salt and oxalate, and avoiding high-dose vitamin C prevent stones.

perOption.r2:c1: Low calcium raises oxalate absorption; normal dietary calcium is advised.
perOption.r2:c2: Low calcium raises oxalate absorption; normal dietary calcium is advised.

caseStudies.title: Missed hemodialysis with hyperkalemia and fluid overload

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 0700
exhibits.body: A 58-year-old client with end-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis Monday, Wednesday and Friday missed Friday and Monday sessions because of transport problems. The client reports weakness, numb hands and shortness of breath lying down. Crackles to mid-lung fields, 3+ ankle edema, jugular veins distended. Left forearm arteriovenous fistula. Weight 84 kg (dry weight 79 kg).

rows.label: ECG
cells: Peaked T waves, wide QRS 0.14 s, flattened P waves

exhibits.title: Home dialysis clinic
exhibits.body: A 49-year-old client does continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (four exchanges a day). Since yesterday the client has had abdominal pain and the drained fluid looks cloudy. The client admits doing exchanges in the kitchen with the window open and the dog nearby, and sometimes skipping the mask. The exit site is red with crusting.

rows.label: Drain volume
cells: Less than the volume instilled for 2 days

caseStudies.title: Acute kidney injury from an NSAID, ACE inhibitor and diuretic

exhibits.title: Medical unit
exhibits.body: A 76-year-old client with hypertension takes lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. For a week the client took ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for knee pain and had diarrhea for 3 days. The client is dizzy and has passed little urine.

caseStudies.title: Infected obstructing kidney stone with urosepsis

exhibits.title: Emergency department
exhibits.body: A 45-year-old client has severe, colicky right flank pain spreading to the groin, nausea, and blood in the urine. Since this morning the client has had shaking chills. CT: a 7 mm stone in the right ureter with hydronephrosis.

rows.label: Urinalysis
cells: Nitrites, many white cells and bacteria
